This study developed and evaluated a model for assessing pain during the surgical period using
photoplethysmogram data from 242 patients. Pain levels were measured at 2 min intervals using a
numerical rating scale or clinical criteria: preoperative, before and after intubation, before and after
skin incision, and postoperative. Key features from the photoplethysmography waveform were
extracted to build XGBoost-based models for intraoperative and postoperative pain assessment.
The combined perioperative model was compared with a commercial surgical pain index, yielding
area under the receiver operating characteristics curve scores of 0.819 and 0.927 for intraoperative
and postoperative periods, respectively, compared to the commercial index ’ss c o r e so f0 . 8 2 9a n d
0.577. These results highlight the models ’ effectiveness in pain assessment throughout the
surgical process, identifying waveform skewness and diastolic phase rate decrease as critical for
intraoperative pain assessment and systolic phase area or baseline ﬂuctuation as signi ﬁcant for
postoperative pain assessment.

Pain is a critical indicator of health, often referred to as theﬁfth vital sign1.
However, because the deﬁnition of pain includes emotional experiences2,
and it is not easy to objectively evaluate pain. Nonetheless, the process of
evaluating pain, especially after surgery, is essential in clinical practice. This
is because managing pain by appropriately administering rescue analgesics
has been shown to improve the patient’sp r o g n o s i s3.T h em o s tc o m m o n l y
used pain assessment method in conscious patients is to ask the patient
directly, using a numerical rating scale (NRS) or visual analog scale.
Although these pain scales are not a method of objectively evaluating pain,
they are useful for evaluating pain occurrence in the recovery room
immediately after surgery. However, a reliable index that could objectively
evaluate pain would have high medical value. Although there are certain
limitations, indices that objectively evaluate intraoperative nociception/
analgesia balance by reﬂecting the degree of activation of the sympathetic
nervous system have already been developed. The surgical pleth index (SPI,
GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) has been used to assess intraoperative
pain based on the inter-pulse interval and amplitude of a
photoplethysmogram (PPG)4. The analgesia nociception index (ANI,
MDoloris Medical Systems, Loos, France) quanti ﬁes analgesia based on
heart rate variability 5. The nociception level (NoL) index (Medasense,
Ramat Gan, Israel) uses a unique multi-parametric sensor platform and
advanced artiﬁcial intelligence algorithms6. Both SPI and ANI are based on
the principle that pain induces discernible alterations in the autonomic
nervous system, providing a quantiﬁable measure of nociception/analgesia
balance. Although it is challenging to accurately evaluate nociception during
general anesthesia, SPI provides a numerical value indicating the need for
additional administration of analgesics7, and studies have shown that SPI-
guided opioid administration could reduce opioid consumption compared
to the conventional methods 8,9. However, even with nociception level-
guided opioid administration, the am ount of remifentanil administered
intraoperatively differed signiﬁcantly depending on the three nociception
monitors used10. This discrepancy seems to stem from differences in the
algorithms of each device for assessing the intraoperative nociception/
analgesia balance during general anesthesia. In addition, the large variation

in the values represented by the nocic eption indices for each individual
makes it dif ﬁcult to titrate opioids. Currently, a demand exists for the
development of an index that can evalu ate intraoperative nociception/
analgesia balance as accurately as possible, and it seems possible to develop a
new model by identifying features that better reﬂect nociception/analgesia
balance than existing indices thro ugh PPG and using machine learning
techniques.
Unlike intraoperatively, conscious patients postoperatively can directly
express their pain. However, although the frequency is low, a few patients
recover after surgery while still intubated. An index that quanti ﬁed pain
objectively and as accurately as possible could help with individualized pain
management for postoperative patients. If postoperative opioids can be
administered based on objective pain indices, there is a possibility that the
amount of postoperative opioids can be reduced, as observed in intrao-
perative studies8,9. Recent studies have reported that unexploited features of
PPG can signi ﬁcantly differentiate postoperative pain 11,12.F e a t u r e st h a t
capture various spatiotemporal aspects, such as changes in area, slope, and
baseline of the PPG waveform, have been correlated with the presence or
absence of postoperative pain11. Furthermore, intra-pulse waveform fea-
tures and dynamic changes in inter-pulse waveform features can inform the
presence or absence of postoperative pain 12.T h e s eﬁndings suggest the
potential for a new model to objectively quantify pain in settings beyond
intraoperative care, offering alternatives to existing methods.
This study has investigated the pre mise that the features critical for
assessing nociception intraoperatively differ from those relevant post-
operatively. Our objective is to develop and validate a nociception assess-
ment model that is effective both intraoperatively and postoperatively,
leveraging a dataset encompassing the perioperative period. Additionally,
we aim to explore the application of arti ﬁcial intelligence techniques to
reﬁne this model.
Results
Feature selection
The top two features derived frommodelintra are min Skew and max PW50/
PPIonset,w h e r eSkew is the skewness of the intra-pulse waveform of PPG,
and PW50/PPIonset is the ratio of the width of a pulse at the point corre-
sponding to 50% amplitude divided by the pulse interval. The top two
features derived frommodelpost are min PAsys and max AVonset,w h e r ePAsys
refers to the systolic area of the waveform from the onset of the pulse until it
reaches its maximum amplitude, and AVonset refers to the amplitude var-
iation between adjacent pulse onsets. The union of the top two features from
modelintra and the top two features from modelpost were used as input fea-
tures formodelperi. A list of key features and the variation in pain assessment
performance by feature combination is described in the Supplementary
Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 1, respectively.
Model Performance
Figure 1 shows the ROC curves of the pain assessment performance of
modelintra, modelpost, modelperi, and the commercially available SPI, with the
average performance across 5-fold cross-validation. In Fig.1a, themodelintra
(area under the receiver operating characteristics curve; AUROC [95%
conﬁdence interval; 95% CI] = 0.807 [0.788–0.828]), modelperi (AUROC =
0.819 [0.779 –0.869]), and SPI (AUROC = 0.829 [0.819 –0.844]) show
similar performance in assessing intraoperative pain. Figure1bs h o w st h a t
modelpost (AUROC = 0.951 [0.932 –0.982]), followed by modelperi
(AUROC = 0.927 [0.892–0.963]), and SPI (AUROC = 0.577 [0.525–0.635]),
performed well in assessing postoperative pain. In the analysis of detailed
evaluation metrics such as accuracy (AC), speciﬁcity (SP), sensitivity (SE),
and positive predictivity value (PPV) (Table1), the modelperi proposed in
this study performed equally or better than SPI both intraoperatively and
postoperatively. Figure2 shows the distribution and median values of the
output values for the pain labels of the proposedmodelperi and the SPI. In the
intraoperative pain assessment results, the median deviation of the output of
modelperi for no pain and pain (Fig.2a) was 31 (=57–26), which is the same
with the deviation of SPI (Fig. 2b) of 31 (=61–30). For postoperative pain
assessment, the output ofmodelperi had a median value of 39 for no pain and
78 for pain (median deviation = 39) (Fig.2c). In contrast, the SPI (Fig.2d)
had a relatively small deviation (7) with median values of 62 for no pain and
69 for pain, and both median values for no pain and pain were above the cut-
off (56), indicating that the model did not adequately separate the two
groups. Figure3 shows the Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values of

Discussion
In this study, we have selected key features from PPG for intraoperative and
postoperative pain assessment, respectively, and developed and validated a

modelperi applicable to both intraoperativeand postoperative pain through
machine learning using the selected key features as input. The developed
model showed acceptable performance (AUROC > 0.8) in both intrao-
perative and postoperative cases. Wh en the nociception criteria became
more stringent, model performance decreased slightly, but the change was
minimal (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). This suggests that the current
model can sensitively capture intraoperative nociception without signiﬁcant
performance degradation, although further research is needed to evaluate
differences in pain severity.
As mentioned earlier, current commercialized pain assessment
methods are recommended for intraoperative use only, and several studies
have reported that they are inadequate for postoperative pain assessment in
conscious patients13–16. Similarly, studies that have assessed postoperative
pain have not conﬁrmed the feasibility of intraoperative pain assessment11,12.
